name: Animals and Puzzle
description: Owl Sonya gave a huge lake puzzle of size n × m to hedgehog Filya as a birthday present. Friends immediately started to assemble the puzzle, but some parts of it turned out to be empty — there was no picture on them. Parts with picture on it are denoted by 1 , while empty parts are denoted by 0 . Rows of the puzzle are numbered from top to bottom with integers from 1 to n , while columns are numbered from left to right with integers from 1 to m . Animals decided to complete the picture and play with it, as it might be even more fun! Owl and hedgehog ask each other some queries. Each query is provided by four integers x 1 , y 1 , x 2 , y 2 which define the rectangle, where ( x 1 , y 1 ) stands for the coordinates of the up left cell of the rectangle, while ( x 2 , y 2 ) stands for the coordinates of the bottom right cell. The answer to the query is the size of the maximum square consisting of picture parts only (only parts denoted by 1 ) and located fully inside the query rectangle. Help Sonya and Filya answer t queries.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains two integers n and m ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 1000 ) — sizes of the puzzle. Each of the following n lines contains m integers a ij . Each of them is equal to 1 if the corresponding cell contains a picture and 0 if it's empty. Next line contains an integer t ( 1 ≤ t ≤ 1 000 000 ) — the number of queries. Then follow t lines with queries' descriptions. Each of them contains four integers x 1 , y 1 , x 2 , y 2 ( 1 ≤ x 1 ≤ x 2 ≤ n , 1 ≤ y 1 ≤ y 2 ≤ m ) — coordinates of the up left and bottom right cells of the query rectangle.
output_specification: Print t lines. The i -th of them should contain the maximum size of the square consisting of 1 -s and lying fully inside the query rectangle.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 713D — Animals and Puzzle [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
